strings.meta.title: Open BitLocker and Linux Drives on macOS — Lukotta
strings.meta.description: Open BitLocker, NTFS, LUKS and Linux drives on your Mac. Type the password and the drive appears in Finder, readable and writable. Free and open source.
strings.meta.ogTitle: Lukotta — BitLocker, Linux and VM disks on macOS
strings.meta.ogDescription: Plug in a drive or open a disk image, type the password, and it appears in Finder, readable and writable, like any other disk.
strings.meta.imageAlt: The Lukotta application icon: a rounded slate square with a letter L cut out of it.
strings.hero.title: Open BitLocker, Linux and virtual machine disks on macOS.
strings.hero.subtitle: Plug in a drive or open a disk image, type the password, and it appears in Finder, readable and writable, like any other disk.
strings.hero.downloadNote: Version {version} · Apple Silicon · macOS 15 Sequoia or later
strings.hero.screenshotAlt: The Lukotta window on macOS, listing the drives connected to the Mac and what each one holds.
strings.opens.title: What it opens
strings.opens.subtitle: Drives your Mac shows as unreadable, and disk images written by virtual machines.
strings.opens.drives.title: Drives
strings.opens.drives.1.def: Unlocked with the volume password or a 48-digit recovery key.
strings.opens.drives.2.def: Including drives Windows left hibernated or did not shut down properly.
strings.opens.drives.3.def: From Linux, both LUKS1 and LUKS2.
strings.opens.drives.4.def: As Ubuntu, Debian, Mint and Fedora set it up. Several volumes on one drive all unlock together.
strings.opens.drives.5.def: ext4, btrfs and XFS, on their own or inside encryption.
strings.opens.images.title: Disk images
strings.opens.images.1.def: qcow2, VMDK, VDI, VHD and VHDX, as VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V, QEMU and UTM write them.
strings.opens.images.2.def: IMG, DMG, and anything else macOS can attach.
strings.opens.images.3.def: A BitLocker or LUKS volume inside any image unlocks exactly as one on a drive does.
strings.opens.note: qcow2, VMDK, VDI and VHD are written as well as read, so files can be copied into a virtual machine's disk without starting the machine.
strings.opens.warning.title: Writing to images is untested
strings.opens.warning.body: The drivers that write qcow2, VMDK, VDI and VHD were written for Lukotta and are checked against qemu-img, but they have not been in use long enough to call thoroughly tested. Open an image read-only to copy files out safely, or make a backup first.
strings.opens.specs: Every format, and what is written and what is not, is specified in SPECS.md.
strings.how.title: How it works
strings.how.subtitle: macOS cannot read BitLocker or Linux filesystems. Linux can. Lukotta starts a small Linux virtual machine, unlocks the drive inside it, and hands the drive back to Finder.
strings.how.1.title: Plug in the drive
strings.how.1.body: Pick it from the list. For a disk image, choose File → Open Disk Image, or File → Open Drive to see every disk attached to this Mac and what Lukotta can do with each.
strings.how.2.title: Type the password
strings.how.2.body: A volume password, a LUKS passphrase, or a 48-digit BitLocker recovery key. Lukotta remembers it in your Keychain when you ask it to.
strings.how.3.title: Open it in Finder
strings.how.3.body: The volume appears under Locations. It reads, writes and ejects like any other drive. Eject it from Lukotta, from the menu bar, or from Finder.
strings.how.networkNote: The drive is handed to Finder over a local network connection, so it appears under Locations with a network icon. macOS offers no way to present it as a local disk.
strings.features.title: Features
strings.features.subtitle: What the application does once a drive is open.
strings.features.1.title: Several drives at once
strings.features.1.body: About ten drives can stay unlocked together, at 30 to 80 MB of RAM each.
strings.features.2.title: Remembers a passphrase
strings.features.2.body: Saved in your Keychain, and only when you ask. Nothing is written to disk in the clear.
strings.features.3.title: Opens again after restarting
strings.features.3.body: Switch it on and Lukotta reopens the drives and images that were open, as they were. It is off until you turn it on.
strings.features.4.title: Hibernated Windows drives
strings.features.4.body: An NTFS volume Windows left dirty or hibernated still opens, rather than being refused.
strings.features.5.title: Thirty-seven languages
strings.features.5.body: Including Arabic and Hebrew, where the interface turns round and reads right to left.
strings.features.6.title: Uninstalls itself completely
strings.features.6.body: One menu item ejects what is open, removes the background helper, deletes the Linux environment, and moves the application to the Bin.
strings.privacy.title: It collects nothing
strings.privacy.body: Lukotta makes one request of its own: a daily check for updates, which can be turned off. There is no account, no telemetry and no analytics. Your passphrase is never written to disk in the clear and never appears in a command line.
strings.permissions.title: What it asks for
strings.permissions.1.def: macOS will not let any application read a drive's raw contents without it. It cannot be requested, so it has to be switched on by hand.
strings.permissions.2.def: Requested by macOS the first time a drive is read.
strings.permissions.3.def: Asked for once, when the background helper is set up. Lukotta never sees it.
strings.requirements.title: Requirements
strings.requirements.1: An Apple Silicon Mac. Intel Macs are not supported.
strings.requirements.3: 260 MB of disk: 160 MB for the application, 100 MB for the Linux environment it unpacks on first use.
strings.requirements.4: 30 to 80 MB of RAM for each drive that is open.
strings.faq.title: Questions
strings.faq.1.a: Nothing. It is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later, and the source is public. There is no paid tier and no account.
strings.faq.2.q: Does it work on an Intel Mac?
strings.faq.2.a: No. Lukotta needs the virtualisation an Apple Silicon Mac provides, and runs on macOS 15 Sequoia or later.
strings.faq.3.q: Why does it need Full Disk Access?
strings.faq.3.a: Reading a drive's raw contents is what unlocking means, and macOS grants no application that access without Full Disk Access. It is a permission macOS will not let an application request, so it has to be switched on by hand in System Settings.
strings.faq.4.q: Why does the drive appear with a network icon?
strings.faq.4.a: The unlocked drive is handed to Finder over a local network connection on your own Mac, which is the only route macOS provides. Nothing leaves the machine. It reads, writes and ejects like any other drive.
strings.faq.5.q: Can it open a drive sealed to a TPM?
strings.faq.5.a: No. A drive sealed to a TPM rather than a password, including Ubuntu's newer hardware-backed encryption, cannot be opened without the machine it belongs to. Neither can a LUKS volume whose header is stored separately from the drive.
strings.faq.6.q: Is it safe to write to a drive?
strings.faq.6.a: Writing to a real drive uses the same Linux drivers your Linux machine uses, and is as safe as writing to it there. Writing to a qcow2, VMDK, VDI or VHD image uses drivers written for Lukotta and is untested; open the image read-only to copy files out, or make a backup first.
strings.faq.7.a: Drives sealed to a TPM, LUKS volumes with a detached header, FileVault and encrypted disk images that macOS opens itself, an image that names another file — a VMware snapshot chain, a differencing VHD, a VHDX with a parent, a qcow2 with a backing file — and a VHDX that was not shut down cleanly.
strings.faq.8.a: No. It never leaves your Mac, is never written to disk in the clear, and never appears in a command line. It is saved in your Keychain only if you ask for it to be.
strings.download.title: Open the drive your Mac says it cannot read.
strings.download.body: Download it, drag it to Applications, and open it. It is signed and notarised.
